§. 3. Nunc in mutua verborum, inter Romanum & Crusium, concertatione videamus, uter utri injuriam dederit. Ac primo quidem ita sentio. Crusium in tota Astri Eclipsi insigni moderatione contra adversarium progressum esse; ut aequi bonique defensor limites, per calumniandi licentiam, praetervectus censeri non debeat; neque enim calumniari praesumitur, qui intorta adversus se convitia ad sui defensionem in adversarium retorquet. Ut apud Juris consultos & Theologos receptum est; sed tum injuriarum reus esse defensor incipit, quando adversario crimina seu vera, seu falsa objicit, quae ad causae Jurisque comprobationem ac defensionem non spectant. Panormitanus in capite cum te. Numero 29. de sententia & re Judicata Joannes Andreas in additionibus ad speculo titulo de injuriis. Angelus in tractatu maleficiis verbo verba contumeliosa Oldradus consilio 53. & Doctores in lege finale Digestis quod quisque juris. & Covarrubias libro 1. variarum resolutiones capitulo 11. numero 7. Praeterea injuriarum tenebitur, si objecta pro sui defensione crimina, quamvis intersit reipublicae ea cognoscere, nequeat tamen probare. quam communem esse sententiam testatur Binsfeldius de injuriis capitulo 1. quaestione 9. conclusione 6. ex Julio Claro & aliis.

§. 4. Porro inter verbi scriptive injurias non habetur, si quis, ab objectis sese

Imò, si quis injuriosis verbis invadenti dixerit, tu mentiris: praesumitur enim Justae defensionis gratia fecisse, per textum in lege quae omnia paragrapho Digestis de procuratoribus. Bartolus & Angelus ibidem. Quod si deinde calumnianti quispiam objecerit, quod calumnietur, multò id magis veniam habet; quia injuriam tantum repellit, cum moderamine inculpatae tutelae. colligitur ex iisdem ad dicta lege autoribus & Castrensi in lege finale Digestis quod quisque juris numero 36. speculator in titulo de accusationibus versiculo quod si te vocavi latronem Panormitanus in dicto capitulo cum te numero 25. Denique in mutuis injuriis dignum cognitu est, quis prior aggressus causam & initium dederit rixae: nam qui defendit, si legitimos fines defensionis non excessit non tenetur de repulsâ injuriâ, ut ex variis legibus Tholosanus probat, Libro 38. syntagmate juris universi capitulo 7. postremò, ut idem capitulo 6. docuit injuria quae literis commendatur, maior iudicanda est, utpotè quae consultò facta sit, & quae diutius perseveret in conspectu hominum. §. 3. Now in the mutual struggle of words between <term>Romanus</term> and <term>Crusius</term>, let us see which of them inflicted injury upon the other. And first, indeed, this is my opinion: that <term>Crusius</term> proceeded against his adversary throughout the *Astri Eclipse* <note>original: "Astri Eclipsi" - likely a satirical work title</note> with notable moderation, so that as a defender of what is fair and good, he should not be considered to have crossed the limits through the license of calumny. For a person is not presumed to be slandering who retorts against an adversary the insults hurled at him for the purpose of his own defense. This is accepted among legal scholars and theologians; but a defender begins to be guilty of injury when he objects to an adversary with crimes, whether true or false, which do not pertain to the proof and defense of the cause and the law. <term>Panormitanus</term> <note>refers to Nicolaus de Tudeschis</note> in chapter *cum te*, number 29, regarding *Sententia & re Judicata* <gloss>judgment and decided matter</gloss>; <term>Joannes Andreas</term> in his additions to the *Speculum* under the title *de injuriis* <gloss>on injuries</gloss>; <term>Angelus</term> <note>refers to Angelus de Ubaldis</note> in his treatise on *maleficiis* <gloss>crimes</gloss> under the word *verba contumeliosa* <gloss>insulting words</gloss>; <term>Oldradus</term> in council 53; and the Doctors in the final law of the *Digestis* <gloss>Digest</gloss> on *quod quisque juris* <gloss>what everyone of right</gloss>; and <term>Covarrubias</term> in book 1 of *variarum resolutionum* <gloss>various resolutions</gloss>, chapter 11, number 7. Furthermore, one will be held for injuries if he cannot prove the crimes objected to for his own defense, even if it is in the interest of the commonwealth to know them, which <term>Binsfeldius</term> attests is the common opinion in *de injuriis*, chapter 1, question 9, conclusion 6, citing <term>Julius Clarus</term> and others.

§. 4. Furthermore, it is not held among written injuries of the word if someone, while protecting themselves from objected

<column-break/>

crimes, says: "It is false what you say." For these words are used even in law as civil terms, such as "you assert falsely" in the law *falso* regarding various rescripts in the *Codice* <gloss>Code</gloss>; "it is falsely persuaded to you" in the law *falso* regarding the common property of others. Indeed, if someone says to an attacker using injurious words, "You are lying," he is presumed to have done so for the sake of just defense, according to the text in the law *quae omnia* paragraph in the *Digestis* regarding *procuratoribus* <gloss>proxies</gloss>. <term>Bartolus</term> and <term>Angelus</term> are of the same opinion there. And if someone thereafter objects to a slanderer that he is slandering, that has even more excuse, because he is merely repelling an injury with the moderation of blameless protection. This is gathered from the same authors on the aforementioned law and from <term>Castrensis</term> in the final law of the *Digestis* on *quod quisque juris*, number 36; <term>Speculator</term> in the title *de accusationibus* <gloss>on accusations</gloss> at the verse "what if I called you a thief"; <term>Panormitanus</term> in the said chapter *cum te*, number 25. Finally, in mutual injuries, it is worth knowing who first attacked and gave the cause and beginning to the brawl; for he who defends, if he did not exceed the legitimate limits of defense, is not held for the repelled injury, as <term>Tholosanus</term> proves from various laws in Book 38 of his *Syntagmate juris universi* <gloss>Treatise on Universal Law</gloss>, chapter 7. Lastly, as the same author taught in chapter 6, an injury that is committed in writing is to be judged greater, inasmuch as it was done deliberately and persists longer in the sight of men. Wherefore, whoever has written, composed, published, or with malicious intent caused a pamphlet, poem, painting, or history to be made for the infamy of someone, is held by the name of injury, paragraph *injuriâ* of *de injuriis*. If a co-heir has purchased land from a creditor.
17. MODESTINUS, Book 9, Rules.
He who has co-heirs, if he has purchased from a creditor <note>original: "(1)"</note> land given as a pledge by his testator, ought not to be summoned by the co-heirs in an action for the division of common property.

Concerning the imposition of a servitude, and the power of the judge.
18. JAVOLENUS, Book 2, Epistles.
An arbiter cannot arrange for hereditary land to serve non-hereditary land <note>original: "(2)"</note>: because the power of the judge cannot exceed that which has been brought into judgment <note>original: "(3)"</note>.
Concerning those things which are on the boundary. 1. Concerning the vestibule. 2. Concerning the road, and the expenses made upon it. 3. Concerning a slave who is in flight. 4. Concerning an aqueduct.
19. PAULUS, Book 6, on Sabinus.
A tree which has grown on the boundary <note>original: "(4)"</note>, likewise a stone which extends through both pieces of land, as long as it adheres to the land, are the property of both parties from the region of their respective boundaries: nor do they come into the action for the division of common property: but when either the stone has been removed, or the tree uprooted or cut down, it shall become common undivided property: and it will come into the action for the division of common property: for that which was in defined parts is again confounded. Wherefore, two masses of two owners having been melted together, the whole mass is common <note>original: "(5)"</note>, even if something from the first form remains separated: thus, a tree and a stone separated from the land confound the right of ownership.
§. 1. An arbiter for the division of common property ought not to be given for a common vestibule <note>original: "(6)"</note> <note>original: "(7)"</note> of two buildings if either party is unwilling: because he who is compelled to bid <note>original: "(8)"</note> for the vestibule necessarily has to set a price for the whole of the buildings at times, if he has no other access <note>original: "(9)"</note>.
§. 2. If a road is owed to us through the same place, and expense has been made upon it, Pomponius says that it is more difficult for an action for the division of common property or an action on partnership to be brought: For what community of right <note>original: "(10)"</note> can be understood separately? But an action for the management of another's affairs <note>original: "(11)"</note> should be brought.

<column-break/>

§. 3. The judge in an action for the division of common property, as also in the action for the division of an inheritance, ought to order those among whom he is the judge to bid for a slave who is in flight <note>original: "(12)"</note>: and then adjudicate him to the one with whom the bidding remained: and there will be no danger that, by decree of the Senate, the penalty of the Fabian law be committed.
§. 4. Labeo says that the right of water passage <note>original: "(13)"</note> does not come into the action for the division of common property: for it is either of the land itself; and therefore does not come into the action: or it is separated from the land, yet divided either by measure or by times <note>original: "(14)"</note>. But rights <note>original: "(15)"</note> can exist even not divided by times: as for instance, when he to whom they belonged left several heirs. When this happens, it is consistent that these also come into the arbitration of the division of an inheritance: nor does Pomponius see why <note>original: "(16)"</note> it should come less into the action for the division of common property than that for the division of an inheritance. Therefore, in cases of this kind, it comes into the action for the division of common property [also], so that the aforementioned rights may be divided either by measure or by times <note>original: "(17)"</note>.

Concerning damage which occurred through the fault of a partner.
20. POMPONIUS, Book 13, on Sabinus.
If he with whom you have common land does not respond to a draft <note>original: "(18)"</note>, and for that reason the villa has been demolished by the movement <note>original: "(19)"</note> of the judge, or trees have been cut down, the loss <note>original: "(21)"</note> will be made good to you <note>original: "(20)"</note> in the action for the division of common property. For whatever is lost by the fault of a partner is contained in that action.

Concerning the office of the Judge.
21. ULPIANUS, Book 30, on Sabinus.
It is fitting for a judge in dividing estates to follow what is most useful <note>original: "(22)"</note> for all, or what the litigants prefer.

If anyone builds in his own name and that of his neighbor.
22. POMPONIUS, Book 33, on Sabinus.
If <note>original: "(23)"</note> I build a wall in my own name and that of my neighbor, whether I intend to seek back the expense from him for his part, or for the sake of a gift <note>original: "(24)"</note>, the wall will become common.

# Choshen Mishpat: Laws of Overcharging and Invalid Sales 226

## Overcharging and Mistake, with 30 sections

226: How much is forgiveness or returning the overcharge, and an agent who made a mistake, and others

1. It is forbidden to overcharge one's neighbor, whether in his purchase or in his sale, and whoever does so—whether buyer or seller—transgresses a negative commandment.

2. How much must the overcharge be for [one] to be obligated to return the money? If he sold [an item] worth six for five, or worth five for six, this is an overcharge, and the purchase stands, and the seller is obligated to return the overcharge to the buyer.

3. If the overcharge was less than this, even a little bit—if he sold worth six for six and a *perutah*—he is not obligated to return anything, for everything less than a sixth is considered forgiven.

4. If the overcharge was more than a sixth, even a little bit—[e.g.,] he sold worth six for five, less a *perutah*—the sale is void, and one can retract it; and similarly, in [every] sale, one can retract if one [party] wishes to accept [the loss].

5. If one sold worth six for five—and there is no overcharge, for there are no "deceivers" [in this case]—...if the overcharge was more than a *perutah*, he must return it; [if] it was a *perutah*, he must return it to his neighbor; if it is less than a sixth, if [the seller] forgives... [the Sages] say: it is permitted for a person to return the money [if he chooses to].

6. Until when can one return and claim the sixth and [cancel] the sale? Until he shows it to a merchant or his relative. And for any [amount] more than that, he can return and claim his overcharge. And if he clarifies that this [item] is known to him, he can investigate within this time [to know] if he was deceived, [and if] he can return and claim, for he [has already] forgiven [it].

7. [Regarding] several serious things, if he returns [the item]...

<column-break/>

10. If he knows about the overcharge, if he leaves the purchase in his hand and he [continues] to use it, the seller has retracted [his claim].
[Regarding] several serious things, if the buyer says: "The purchase is in my hand and I will use it," the seller has retracted [his claim].

11. There is no need to say regarding the cancellation of a purchase, where he does not know the value [of the item] until he shows it to a merchant. Therefore, if the purchase was an item that does not change [in value], such as pepper and similar [things], if he did not claim it, he cannot return and claim, for he has forgiven [it].

12. If he sold because of his distress and he sold it for less than the value [of] the mistake, [because] he sold [it] due to distress, he cannot return [it] and [the buyer] is forgiven.

13. [If] he sold worth four for five, the sale is void, and he did not manage to show it to a merchant or his relative, and now [the value] stands at the buyer's price, he can retract it, [but] the seller cannot [claim] "I have profited," [if] he has not [yet] realized the profit.

14. Similarly, [if] a seller [sold] worth five for four, and it stands at the buyer's price, the seller can retract [the sale], and the buyer cannot say to the seller: "Not because of me [the price] changed," [for he can] retract [the sale] if he has not [yet] realized the profit.

15. [If] he sold worth five for six, and he did not manage to show it until it increased and stood at [its new] price, the seller is obligated to return [it], and [he is] obligated to return [it] if it increased in the buyer's domain.

16. Similarly, if he sold six for five, and the price dropped to four, the buyer is obligated to return [the difference] to the seller, for the sale was acquired and [it] dropped in the buyer's domain.

<header>OF PELAGIUS.</header>

THE PASSION OF SAINT PELAGIUS, THE MOST PRECIOUS MARTYR, WHO WAS CROWNED BY MARTYRDOM IN CORDOBA IN OUR TIMES.

ARGUMENT CONCERNING THE SAME.

Abdrahemen, the tyrant of Mauritania, following the sect of the Saracens, crossed into Spain and subjected all Christians to punishments or forced them into his sect. When he had taken Corduba, the distinguished city of Spain, he killed the elders of the city or accepted money for them. And when he had imposed such a great sum of money upon a noble citizen, which he could not pay to the tyrant, and was due to be led to prison, his son, moved first by piety, submitted to chains for him. Because of whose beauty, when it had been related to the tyrant, the youth is led from prison; he offers him to the tyrant so that he might yield to his lust. And when the tyrant pressed the youth with many prayers, the youth yields his kisses to the tyrant, the youth seeking with his fist. The tyrant, the youth's embraces refusing, threw him over the wall with a sling and a ballista into the river that washes Corduba. His body, struck by the rocky banks, is collected by fishermen and truncated by the tyrant's satellites. Finally, he is buried most religiously by the citizens.

PREFACE OF HROTSVITHA ON PELAGIUS:

Do not, Pelagius, most brave martyr of Christ,
And good soldier of the King reigning through the ages,
Look with mild piety upon me, Hrotsvitha, a miserable one,
A maid devoted to you with a mind subject to you.
Whom I worship in my mind, and bring forth a song from my breast,
And may it be watered by the dew from above of my small
Breast, the dark cave now, I pray, more mercifully,
So that I may be able to worthily and marvelously record your praises,
And sign your famous triumph with my pen,
And whom you nobly conquered, the world with bloody death,
Having purchased a shining palm with your blood.
